2.3a — Health Potions & the Max-Health Cap

You can take damage; now undo it. But healing without a cap breaks the game — the potion becomes god mode. Today: your first real if statement, protecting a rule the game designer cares about.

Predict First ~10 min

The starter has coins (trigger, +1) and spikes (collision, −1). It has no potion. Predict the two bugs a naive potion causes before you write anything:

  1. You have 3 health, drink 5 potions. What number is health? Should it be? What does the Console say vs what the game should say?
  2. At what health value does drinking a potion stop matter — and should it still "work"? (A designer question: is a wasted potion annoying or fair?)

The AP exam calls this selection — an if that changes behavior based on a condition. You have technically seen ifs already (the tag checks); this is the first one that encodes a rule instead of an identity. Same keyword, different job.

Build Lab ~25 min

Step 1 — the potion object. Make a Potion from the pickup pattern: a GameObject with a SpriteRenderer (any distinctive sprite), a BoxCollider2D with Is Trigger checked, and the tag Potion (add it in the tag list). Drag it to Assets/Prefabs to make it a prefab, like the Coin.

Step 2 — the naive version. In PlayerController.OnTriggerEnter2D, add a branch:

if (other.CompareTag("Potion"))
{
    if (StatManager.manager != null)
    {
        StatManager.manager.ChangeHealth(1);
    }
    Destroy(other.gameObject);
}

Run it, heal to full, keep drinking. Watch the Console. Health is now 6, 7, 8 — the game's rule is gone. You built the exploit yourself, on purpose. Fixing it comes next.

Step 3 — the cap. Two ways to say "never more than 3":

// Option A: guard inside StatManager.ChangeHealth
public void ChangeHealth(int amount)
{
    health += amount;
    if (health > 3)
    {
        health = 3;
    }
    Debug.Log("Health Changed! New Health: " + health);
    ...
}

// Option B: the Math class
health = Mathf.Min(health, 3);

Read both. Which object should own the cap — the potion (it heals), the player (it gets healed), or the StatManager (it owns health)? The starter's answer is the StatManager, because the rule protects health, and health is the StatManager's job. Everything that touches health must obey the same cap — that is the whole argument for putting the rule in one place.

Bug Hunt: Overheal and friends

  1. What happens if the cap is > 3 but health starts at 3 and you drink at exactly full? Trace it line by line.
  2. Change the cap to < 1 in the wrong direction — say if (health < 1) { health = 1; }. Now spike yourself to zero. What rule did you just invent?
  3. Put the cap in the potion branch instead of ChangeHealth. Why is that the same today but fragile the moment a second healing item appears?
  4. What does Mathf.Min(health, 3) return when health is −2? Is the min cap enough for the whole system — or do you also need the death check to catch it?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Design the economy

  1. Should a potion be worth 1 health or 2? Make potions spawn rarely and be worth 2 — what breaks, and what does "rare" mean in a level design sense?
  2. Turn the max into a [SerializeField] so you can tune maxHealth in the Inspector like xSpeed. Where exactly do you declare it — and what replaces every hardcoded 3 in ChangeHealth?
  3. Hard: full health + potion = wasted. Make the potion NOT be destroyed if it heals nothing. What does the player feel, and which line did you touch?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Build a pickup object with trigger + custom tag from scratch
  • Explain selection: the if that encodes a rule vs the if that checks identity
  • Argue where a rule belongs (StatManager vs the item) and why
  • Trace an overheal exploit and cap it two ways
